<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/explanation/philosophy -->

Gram is an open-source declarative DSL (*Domain-Specific Language*) for cooking recipes, built for developers and culinary craftsmen.

Most recipe formats are just static blocks of text. Gram takes a fundamentally different approach: it takes your instructions written in plain text and compiles them into structured, calculated, relational, and schedulable data.

## The philosophy

Cooking is a bit like an algorithm: you take raw ingredients as input and output a finished dish. But to me, it's above all a passion. That's where Gram comes from: I love cooking, and I wanted a tool that combines the rigor of code with creativity in the kitchen. 

I've always loved the idea of writing recipes in plain text, heavily inspired by pioneering projects like the excellent [Cooklang](https://cooklang.org). Cooklang is fantastic for quick, straightforward home recipes. But when things get a bit more complex—like professional pastry formulas with multiple sub-components, baker's math, or tricky scheduling—relying entirely on natural language can get messy. 

Gram also draws structural inspiration from the classic [Cooking for Engineers](http://www.cookingforengineers.com/) tabular format. Because Gram compiles recipes into a deterministic JSON tree, it natively unlocks advanced visual presentations: production run sheets, interactive Gantt timelines, tabular flowcharts, and calendar exports.

I created Gram as an alternative for these more demanding scenarios. It introduces **relational logic**, **physical accuracy**, **modular composition**, and **predictive scheduling** into your recipe writing:

- **Relational Variables**: If you make a dough in step 1, you can reference it as an ingredient in step 5, cleanly preventing duplication or manipulation ambiguity.
- **Physical Accuracy & Calculations**: Gram understands the difference between the "zest of 1 lemon" and "juice of 2 lemons", ensuring your shopping list accurately aggregates to "Buy 2 lemons" instead of 3. It also computes real physical mass and relative ingredient ratios (`70% @&flour`).
- **Strict Data Contracts**: By using explicit tags (`@`, `~`, `^`, `#`), Gram ensures that temperatures, durations, ingredients, and cookware are never confused by the parser.
- **Modularity & Reusability (`@use`)**: Split shared bases (pastries, stocks, sauces) into their own `.gram` files. Gram seamlessly inlines their steps, automatically scales their quantities to match what your dish asks for (it measures the base's own mass — no manual scaling to declare or keep in sync), and merges their raw ingredients onto your unified shopping list.
- **ALAP Scheduling & Retro-planning**: Calculate the exact moment to start each step so everything converges at service time, optimize masked time during passive cooking or chilling, and anticipate cookware bottlenecks.

:::tip[The Ecosystem Approach]
Gram isn't just a syntax; it's a complete ecosystem for building culinary applications.
If you're building a recipe app, a meal planner, or a smart kitchen dashboard, you shouldn't have to parse raw text manually. The **Gram Engine** processes your text into a rich Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), enriches it with physical properties (like mass standardization and nutrition), schedules production workflows, and outputs a reliable JSON structure you can actually work with.
:::


## Designed for developers

The Gram ecosystem gives you everything you need to treat recipes like software:


  ### Parser & Compiler

    **`@gram-lang/kitchen`**: Simulates the execution timeline, composes `@use` modules, aggregates base shopping lists, and scales dynamic quantities.
  
  ### Scheduling Engine

    **`@gram-lang/scheduler`**: Computes ALAP retro-planning, optimizes mise en place placement, resolves equipment contention, and projects recipes onto a real-world calendar.
  
  ### Semantic Analyzer

    **`@gram-lang/analyzer`**: Handles mass standardization, yield calculation, nutritional estimation, and advanced shopping list aggregation based on your local database.
  
  ### Language Server (LSP)

    **`@gram-lang/language-server`**: Brings proper editor support to recipes (autocompletion, diagnostics, hover tooltips).
  
  ### CLI

    **`@gram-lang/cli`**: Compile, scale, schedule, diff, and manage your ingredient database straight from your terminal.
  
  ### Renderer

    **`@gram-lang/renderer`**: Instantly generate Semantic HTML, Gantt charts, production run sheets, and Markdown from your compiled JSON.
  


## How it looks

Gram remains highly readable, but quietly introduces some powerful data structures. Here is a look at a classic French pastry recipe written in Gram:

<CodeTabs>
```gram title="canneles.gram"
---
title: 'Cannelés'
portions: 10
---

## Batter ~{-1d} ->&batter

[Mix] In a #mixing bowl{}, combine the @flour{300 g}, @sugar{500 g}, and @salt{3 g}. ->&dry ingredients{}

[Heat] In a #large saucepan{}, bring the @milk{1 l}, @butter{100 g}, and @vanilla bean{1}(split and scraped) to ^{85C}. ->&hot milk{}

[Mix] Pour the &hot milk{} over the &dry ingredients{} all at once. Whisk vigorously.

[Incorporate] Add the @egg yolks{6}<@eggs{6} and the @rum{100 ml}.

[Chill] Cover with #plastic wrap{} touching the surface and chill in the refrigerator for at least ~_refrigerator{24 h}.
```
```json title="Output Glimpse"
{
  "title": "Cannelés",
  "meta": { "portions": "10" },
  "generator": "@gram-lang/kitchen@1.4.0",
  "metrics": {
    "preparationTime": 24,
    "activeTime": 41,
    "totalMass": 2132,
    "nutrition": {
      "total": {
        "calories": 4927,
        "protein": 80.2,
        "carbs": 781.6
        // ...
      }
    }
  },
  "miseEnPlace": [
    { "section": 0, "duration": 9, "items": [ { "kind": "gather", "target": "ingredient", "count": 7, "duration": 7 } /* ... */ ] }
    // ...
  ],
  "tasks": { "tasks": [ /* ... */ ], "sections": [ /* ... */ ] },
  "schedule": {
    "miseEnPlace": "perSection", "rests": "shortest",
    "totalTime": 1465, "activeTime": 56, "preparationTime": 9, "idleTime": 1400,
    "blocks": [ { "kind": "prep", "task": "s0.prep", "section": 0, "start": 0, "end": 9 } /* ... */ ]
  },
  "shopping_list": [
    {
      "id": "flour",
      "qty": 300,
      "unit": "g",
      "normalizedMass": 300,
      "conversionMethod": "physical"
    },
    // ...
    {
      "type": "composite",
      "id": "eggs",
      "qty": 6,
      "usage": [ { "id": "egg-yolks", "qty": 6, "normalizedMass": 102 } ]
    }
  ],
  "sections": [
    {
      "title": "Batter",
      "retro_planning": { "raw": "-1d", "sign": -1, "value": 1, "unit": "d", "minutes": -1440 },
      "intermediate_preparation": "batter",
      "steps": [
        {
          "type": "step",
          "action": "Mix",
          "content": [
            "In a ",
            { "id": "mixing-bowl", "_usageId": "36", "fixed": false },
            ", combine the ",
            { "id": "flour", "qty": 300, "unit": "g", "normalizedMass": 300 },
            // ... (rest of the parsed AST)
          ]
        }
        // ... (other steps)
      ]
    }
    // ... (other sections)
  ]
}
```
</CodeTabs>

Notice how the `[Incorporate]` step uses `<@eggs{6}`? This *composite ingredient* syntax tells Gram that you are only using the yolks, but the shopping list should correctly aggregate the whole eggs required. The `~{-1d}` section tag creates a retro-planning schedule relative to the final baking time, and `->&hot milk{}` sets up an intermediate variable you can pour later.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/document-structure -->

A Gram recipe file (`.gram`) is structured into several distinct parts: Metadata, Sections, Steps, and Comments.

## 1. Metadata (frontmatter)

The frontmatter is a **YAML** block at the very start of the file, enclosed by `---`.

The Gram parser accepts **any** key-value pair in this block. You can add custom fields for your own application's needs. However, the Gram Compiler recognizes two types of keys: **Functional** and **Informational**.

### Functional keys
These keys directly alter how the Gram Compiler processes the recipe:

*   `portions`: (Integer) The baseline number of servings. Divides the [Nutritional Estimation](/docs/explanation/nutrition) into per-portion figures, and is rescaled alongside quantities when a recipe is scaled — so per-portion values stay the same whatever factor you apply. A trailing label (`portions: 4 servings`) is tolerated; a zero or negative count is ignored.
*   `densities`: (Object) Custom density overrides for specific `@ingredient` items, used by the [Mass Standardization](/docs/explanation/engine/kitchen) algorithm.

### Informational keys
These keys are recommended for proper display and metadata management:

*   `title`: The recipe name.
*   `description`: A short summary (useful for SEO meta tags).
*   `tags`: A list of categories or keywords.
*   `category`: Main category (e.g. "Dessert", "Main Course").
*   `author`: Name or list of authors.
*   `source`: URL(s) to the original recipe.
*   `date`, `lastUpdated`: YYYY-MM-DD.
*   `makes`: The physical output or dimensions of the recipe (e.g., "1 layer cake", "24 cookies", "20x20cm mold").
*   `notes`: General notes about the recipe (e.g. "Tested on 2026-06-07. Decrease sugar next time.").

<CodeTabs>
```gram title="recipe.gram"
---
title: 'Matcha Brownies'
description: 'A simple Japanese-style matcha brownie...'
author: ["Auguste Kerflec"]
tags: ['brownie', 'matcha']
category: 'Dessert'
source: ['https://example.com/matcha-brownie']
makes: '20x20cm mold'

# Functional Fields
portions: 4
densities:
  - flour: 0.55
---
```
</CodeTabs>

## 2. Module imports

*(since v1.2.0)*

Right after the frontmatter, before any step, a recipe can `@use` other `.gram` files as reusable sub-components.

```gram
@use "./bases/pate-sablee.gram" as &pate

## Montage

[Foncer] le moule avec &pate{250g}.
```

*See [Module Imports](/docs/reference/syntax/modules) for the full syntax, scaling rules, and encapsulation guarantees.*

## 3. Steps

Each paragraph in a Gram file represents a single cooking step. Steps are separated by one or more empty lines.

```gram
A step,
the same step.

A different step.
```

### Action verbs
Steps can optionally start with an **Action** enclosed in brackets `[]`. This highlights the primary method used in that step, making it easy to parse visually or programmatically.

```gram
[Mix] The @flour and @water.

[Bake] In the #oven for ~{30min}.
```

## 4. Sections

Complex recipes often have multiple components (e.g., dough, filling, frosting) that are prepared separately. You can group steps into `## Section` blocks using Markdown-style headings (e.g., `## Dough`).

```gram
## Dough

Mix @flour{200g} and @water{100ml} together until smooth.

## Filling

Combine @cheese{100g} and @spinach{50g}, then season to taste.
```

### Retro-planning (scheduling)
You can assign a preparation timeframe to a `## Section` by adding a `~timer`-like annotation anywhere in the title.

```gram
## Puff Pastry ~{-2d}
```
This tells the compiler that the "Puff Pastry" `## Section` should be prepared **2 days in advance**.
Supported suffixes are `d` (days), `h` (hours), `min` or `m` (minutes) — free text (e.g. `~{the day before}`) is not valid here and is flagged by the compiler.

*See [Times & Scheduling](/docs/reference/syntax/times#section-retro-planning) for the full syntax rules and error handling.*

### Section outputs (declarations)
If a `## Section` produces a sub-component that will be used later in the recipe, you can declare it using `->&` at the end of the title.

```gram
## Puff Pastry ->&dough
```
*See [Intermediate Variables](/docs/reference/syntax/intermediate-variables) for more details.*

## 5. Comments

You can add comments to explain instructions without affecting the compiled output.

**Inline Comments (`//`)**:
```gram
Mash @potato{2kg} until smooth // alternatively, boil 'em first.
```

**Block Comments (`/* ... */`)**:
```gram
Slowly add @milk{4 cup} /* TODO change units to litres */, keep mixing.
```

:::note[Comments vs YAML Notes]
Comments are preserved during compilation and are rendered alongside the instructions (typically in grey italics). They are perfect for small, step-specific tips. However, if you have global observations or general feedback about the recipe (e.g., "Decrease sugar next time", "Best served cold"), it is recommended to put them in the YAML Frontmatter under the `notes` key so they can be displayed prominently at the top.
:::

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/ingredients -->

Ingredients are the core building blocks of any Gram recipe.

## Basic declaration

To declare an `@ingredient`, use the `@` symbol. If the `@ingredient` name contains spaces or requires a specific quantity, you **must** append the quantity inside `{}` braces. If it is a single word without a specific quantity, the braces are optional (the quantity defaults to 1).

```gram
[Add] @salt and @ground black pepper{} to taste.

[Poke] Holes in @potatoes{2}.
```

:::note
`@ingredient` names can contain special characters (like `'`, `&`, `.`), except for the dedicated syntax delimiters (`{`, `}`, `:`, `(`, `)`, `<`, `|`).
:::

### Units
To specify a unit of measurement (weight, volume, etc.), add it directly after the numeric value inside the braces, separated by an optional space.

```gram
[Place] @bacon strips{1kg} on a baking sheet and glaze with @syrup{1/2 tbsp}.
```

A unit can be several words (`{2 tablespoons}`) and can contain dots or apostrophes (`{1 c.à.s}`, `{1 c. à s.}`). Common spellings of the same unit are recognized as equivalent: `c.à.s`, `c.a.s` and `càs` all mean tablespoon in French.

:::caution
A quantity in braces that can't be read (`@salt{1 g/l}`, or a brace that is never closed) stops parsing with an error pointing at the offending brace.
:::

## Scaling & fixed quantities

By default, the Gram Compiler scales an `@ingredient` **linearly** based on the number of portions requested. 
If you scale a recipe from 2 to 4 servings, an `@ingredient` with `{100g}` becomes `{200g}`.

### Fixed quantities (`=`)
Some `@ingredient` items (like salt, yeast, or spices) should not scale linearly. You can lock their quantity using the `=` modifier.

```gram
Season with @=salt{1 tsp} to taste.
```
This keeps the salt at 1 tsp regardless of how many servings the user calculates.

## Ingredient modifiers

Gram provides several modifiers to alter how an `@ingredient` behaves in the parser and the shopping list. Modifiers are placed immediately after the `@` symbol.

| Modifier | Name | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `&` | **Reference** | References an `@ingredient` previously declared. Does NOT add it to the shopping list again. |
| `=` | **Fixed** | Marks the quantity as fixed (it will not scale with portions). |
| `?` | **Optional** | Marks the `@ingredient` as optional. |
| `-` | **Hidden** | Hides the `@ingredient` from the generated shopping list. |
| `*` | **Baker's %** | Marks the `@ingredient` as the reference (100%) to calculate baker's percentages. |

:::caution[Combining Modifiers]
You can combine modifiers (e.g., `@?-thyme`). However, absurd combinations (e.g. `?*`, `-*`, `-&`) or duplicates (`**`) will generate a compiler warning (`INVALID_MODIFIER_COMBINATION`).
:::

### Optional and hidden modifiers (`?`, `-`)

Use `?` to mark an `@ingredient` as optional — useful for garnishes or substitutions the cook may skip. Use `-` to hide an `@ingredient` from the generated shopping list entirely, e.g. something you always have on hand.

```gram
[Garnish] Sprinkle with @?thyme{} and a pinch of @-salt{} to taste.
```

### The reference modifier (`&`)

The reference modifier is crucial for multi-step recipes. **As a best practice, any time you mention an `@ingredient` after its initial declaration, you should use the `&` modifier.**

The compiler's behavior changes depending on whether you provide a new quantity with your reference:

1. **Pure Reference (No Quantity)**
When instructing the user to use an already declared `@ingredient`, use `@&` so it isn't counted twice in the shopping list.
```gram
[Add] @flour{200g} to the bowl.

[Dust] The work surface with the @&flour.
```

2. **Additive Reference (With Quantity)**
Sometimes you need to use the *same* `@ingredient` multiple times with *different* additions throughout the recipe. Using `@&ingredient{qty}` tells the compiler: "This is the same `@ingredient`, please add this extra quantity to the total shopping list."
```gram
[Add] @butter{100g} to the dough.

[Grease] Use @&butter{50g} to grease the pan. // The shopping list will correctly aggregate 150g of butter.
```

### Baker's percentage (`*`)

In baking, recipes are often built around the **Baker's Percentage**, where the main `@ingredient` (usually flour) represents 100%, and all other items are expressed as a percentage of that weight.

Gram provides a dedicated modifier to mark the reference `@ingredient`. By placing a `*` after the `@` symbol, you tell the Gram Compiler: *"This is the 100% reference point"*.

```gram
[Add] The @*flour{500g}, @water{350g} and @salt{10g}.
```

This allows tools (like the CLI or web renderers) to automatically calculate and display the baker's percentages for all other items (e.g., Water: 70%, Salt: 2%) without you having to define them manually as relative quantities.

:::note
For a full guide on leveraging this feature, see the [How to Scale Recipes Dynamically](/docs/how-to/scale-recipes#bakers-math) guide.
:::

## Advanced syntax

### Short-hand preparations
Often, an `@ingredient` requires preparation before use. You can define this directly within the declaration using parentheses `()`.

```gram
[Mix] @butter{1 stick}(room temperature) and @garlic{2 cloves}(peeled and minced).
```

:::tip[Best Practice: Inline vs Full Steps]
Gram encourages writing dense, data-oriented recipes. Instead of creating dedicated steps for basic *mise-en-place* tasks (e.g., `[Peel] The garlic.` then `[Mince] The garlic.`), it is highly recommended to declare these states inline using `(...)`. This keeps your recipe concise, avoids polluting the step flow, and allows frontend renderers to cleanly group preparations in the ingredient list!
:::

:::note[Where a preparation counts]
Each preparation counts toward the mise en place of **its own section**, where it adds 2 minutes. In the HTML view, a "Mise en place" label on the section's ingredient list shows that its preparation happens there; hover it for the detail. See [When the mise en place happens](/docs/reference/syntax/times#when-the-mise-en-place-happens).
:::

:::caution[Spacing is strict]
The preparation parenthesis `(...)` MUST be immediately adjacent to the quantity braces `{...}` (or to the name if there are no braces). Do not add a space between them, otherwise it will be parsed as plain text.
:::

### Component alias (renaming)
You can rename an `@ingredient` for display purposes using a colon `:` immediately after the real name. This is useful for keeping the shopping list clean while using a colloquial name in the instructions.

**Format**: `@Real Name:Display Name{Quantity}`

<CodeTabs>
```gram title="Code"
Deglaze with @dry white wine:wine{100ml}.
```
```markdown title="Rendered Recipe"
1. Deglaze with **wine** (100ml).
```
```markdown title="Shopping List"
- **dry white wine**: 100ml
```
</CodeTabs>

The shopping list will aggregate this under "dry white wine", but the rendered recipe will just say "wine".

:::tip[Re-using aliased ingredients]
Aliases are applied locally. To mention this same `@ingredient` again later in the recipe, you must reference its **real name**, not the alias (e.g. `@&dry white wine`). If you write `@wine`, Gram will treat it as a brand new `@ingredient`.
:::

:::tip[Not the same as a database alias]
This `:` syntax only renames how the ingredient is *displayed* in the rendered steps — it never affects shopping-list grouping. The shopping list and the canonical ingredient id are always derived from the **real name** (before the colon), matched against `ingredients.yaml`'s own `aliases` list — a separate, database-level mechanism used to merge synonyms and cross-language duplicates (e.g. `sugar`/`sucre`/`azúcar`) across recipes, see [Manage an Ingredient Database](/docs/how-to/manage-database). Writing `@egg yolks:eggs{2}` and `@egg whites:eggs{4}` will **not** merge them in the shopping list, even though they share the same display alias `eggs` — they have different real names.
:::

### Alternatives (substitutions)
You can define acceptable alternatives for an `@ingredient` using the pipe `|` operator.

```gram
Add @milk{100ml}|@water{95ml}.
```
This works with short-hand preparations as well:
```gram
@onion{1}(peeled and chopped)|@shallots{2}(minced)
```

### Ranges
Recipes aren't always exact. You can specify a range using a hyphen `-`.

```gram
Add @eggs{2-4}.

Pour @water{1.5-2l}.
```

### Fractions
Quantities accept fractions in three forms — a plain fraction, a mixed number, or a Unicode fraction glyph — all normalized to the same decimal value.

```gram
Add @sugar{1/2 cup}.

Add @flour{1 1/2 cups}.

Add @butter{1½ sticks}.
```

## Error handling

Some syntax errors stop the recipe from being read before it is even compiled: an unreadable quantity in braces (`@salt{1 g/l}`), a brace that is never closed. The message points at the exact spot to fix, and the editor underlines it.

The compiler checks for semantic errors in your `@ingredient` declarations and will output specific warnings:

- **Invalid Modifier**: If you combine incompatible modifiers (like `?*`), the compiler warns `INVALID_MODIFIER_COMBINATION` and ignores them.
- **Undefined Reference**: If you use a reference (`@&ingredient`) but that item hasn't been declared previously in the recipe, the compiler warns `UNDEFINED_REFERENCE`.
- **Database Missing**: If you compile with a database and the `@ingredient` is not found, it warns `MISSING_INGREDIENT`.
- **Missing Macros**: If the database lacks nutritional information for the `@ingredient`, it warns `MISSING_MACROS`.
- **Unknown Mass**: If it cannot convert a volume or count into grams to estimate nutrition, it warns `UNKNOWN_MASS`.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/cookware -->

You can define the tools and equipment needed for a recipe using the `#` symbol.

## Basic declaration

Like an `@ingredient`, if the `#cookware` name is a single word and you only need one of it, you can omit the braces `{}`.

```gram
Heat the #pan.
```

If the name contains spaces or you want to specify a quantity, you must use braces `{}`.

```gram
Take a #baking sheet{}.
```

## Quantities vs dimensions

Unlike an `@ingredient` (which supports continuous units such as grams or milliliters), `#cookware` maintains a strict syntactic separation between its **count** and its **physical description**.

**Quantities (counts)**

The braces `{}` are strictly reserved for the number of items needed. This must be an integer count:

```gram
#pan              // Defaults to 1 pan
#ramekins{4}      // 4 ramekins
```
  **Dimensions & materials**

To specify size, diameter, material, or surface characteristics, use parentheses `()`:

```gram
#pan(20cm)                  // 1 pan, sized 20cm
#baking sheet{2}(non-stick) // 2 baking sheets, non-stick
```

:::caution
Do not put dimensions inside quantity braces (e.g. ❌ `#pan{20cm}`). Gram expects a pure integer inside `{}`. Use parentheses instead: ✅ `#pan(20cm)`.
:::

## Scaling behavior

Unlike an `@ingredient` which scales proportionally by default, `#cookware` scaling depends on whether an explicit quantity was declared:

| Format | Example | Scaling type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **No quantity** | `#pan` | [Fixed] | Does not change when portions increase. |
| **With quantity** | `#pan{1}` or `#ramekins{4}` | [Scalable] | Doubling portions asks for 2 pans or 8 ramekins. |
| **Explicit fixed** | `#=pan{2}` | [Fixed] | Stays fixed at 2 pans even if the recipe is scaled up. |

## Modifiers and advanced syntax

`#cookware` supports several of the advanced syntax mechanisms available for ingredients:

**Modifiers**

You can apply Optional (`?`), Hidden (`-`), Fixed (`=`), and Reference (`&`) modifiers directly after `#`:

```gram
Use a #?wok if you have one, otherwise a #-large pan will do.

Return to the #&wok to finish the sauce.
```
  **Component alias**

You can rename an equipment item for display while keeping a clean canonical slug using the `:` operator:

```gram
Use the #cast iron skillet:skillet{}.
```
  **Alternatives**

You can declare acceptable equipment substitutions using the pipe `|` operator:

```gram
Cook in a #pan|#wok.
```

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/times -->

You can define `~timer` declarations and durations in your recipes using the `~` symbol.

## Basic declaration

A `~timer` **must** specify an explicit unit inside the braces. Fuzzy prose such as `~{about 10 minutes}` is invalid and rejected by the parser.

```gram
Bake for ~{25min}.
```

**Supported units:**
- `min` (minutes) - Canonical preferred standard.
- `h` (hours).
- `d` (days).
- `s` (seconds).

:::note
Shorthand `m` or the word `minutes` are automatically normalized to `min` by the compiler.
:::

These units are resolved through Gram's multi-language time dictionary: localized aliases below are recognized natively regardless of the recipe language (e.g. in a French recipe, `~{2j}` resolves identically to `~{2d}`).

| Canonical | Aliases |
| --- | --- |
| `d` | `day`, `days` |
| `h` | `hour`, `hours` |
| `m` | `min`, `mins`, `minute`, `minutes` |
| `s` | `sec`, `secs`, `second`, `seconds` |

### Timer names
You can assign an explicit name to a `~timer`. This is especially useful for passive background tasks: when multiple timers run concurrently (like a dough fermenting while a stock simmers), named timers allow user interfaces and production run sheets to track each process simultaneously without confusion.

```gram
Boil @eggs{2} for ~eggs{3min}.
```

### Exact times and ranges
*(since v1.4.0)*

By default, a timer is **exact**: `~_{12h}` lasts exactly 12 hours. When an operation has variable or flexible duration, specify an interval: this provides official elasticity for Gram's scheduling engine.

```gram
Let the dough rest in the fridge ~_{12-24h}.

Roast the chicken for ~{40-50min}.
```

The interpretation of a range differs fundamentally based on timer type:

- **A passive range represents elasticity.** The declaration `~_{12-24h}` states: "ready from 12 hours, optimal up to 24 hours". By default, the timeline lays out the shortest bound (`'shortest'`). You can select alternative elasticity strategies (`'shortest'`, median `'balanced'`, or longest `'longest'`) via the `--rests` CLI option, the `gram.rests` VS Code setting, or the `rests` renderer option. When provided with a target serving time and kitchen availability, the scheduler uses this elasticity to bridge overnight non-working hours without requiring cook intervention (see [Planning in real time](/docs/explanation/planning-in-real-time/)).
- **An active range represents operational uncertainty.** The declaration `~{40-50min}` represents how long the chicken takes to roast. The schedule always defaults to the longest bound (50 minutes) so that service is never delayed. Passive elasticity settings (`rests`) do not apply to active timers.

:::note
Deprecated fields of the compiled recipe (`steps[].timings`, `steps[].backgroundTasks`, and `metrics`) continue to evaluate ranges as their average value until version 2.0.0. Consume the modern `schedule` blocks instead.
:::

## Active vs passive

The Gram compiler builds a complete execution timeline (similar to a Gantt chart) for each recipe. To achieve realistic scheduling, it distinguishes hands-on kitchen work from autonomous background tasks.

:::tip[💡 The Golden Rule: Does this step block YOU from starting the next step?]

| Cook Status | Timer Type | Syntax | Culinary Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **YES** (Exclusive manual attention required) | **Active** | `~` | *Whisking by hand, stirring risotto, plating* |
| **NO** (Equipment or time does the work) | **Passive** | `~_` | *Oven baking, fermentation, simmering, chilling* |

:::

### Active (default)
By default, a `~timer` is active. It requires direct hands-on involvement: the step is **blocking** and demands undivided attention before moving on to subsequent operations.

```gram
Whisk the @heavy cream{} continuously for ~{5min}.
```
> ⏱️ **Result:** Adds 5 minutes to **active time**.

### Passive (`_`)
Add the `_` modifier to designate a passive `~timer`. This represents a **background task**. You initiate the timer (e.g. putting a dish into the oven) and can immediately proceed with subsequent steps.

```gram
Bake in the #oven for ~_{45min}.

Meanwhile, prepare the glaze...
```
> ⏱️ **Result:** Adds 0 minutes to active time, but extends **idle / passive duration** to ensure these 45 minutes elapse before removing the dish.

### Sequential passive timers (named tracks)
By default, passive timers run concurrently with the rest of the recipe. However, certain background operations sharing equipment cannot physically overlap (e.g. blind-baking a crust for 10 minutes, then lowering the heat and continuing baking for 30 minutes in the same oven).

To enforce **sequential** execution of passive timers, assign them the **same track name**:

```gram
Bake in the #oven at 240°C for ~_baking{10min}.

Lower the heat to 180°C and bake for ~_baking{30min}.
```

> ⏱️ **Result:** Because both timers share the track name `baking`, Gram places them on the same background track. The 30-minute timer will only start *after* the 10-minute timer completes. Idle waiting time increases by 40 minutes, while active hands-on time remains zero.

## How time is calculated

Behind the scenes, Gram tracks four distinct time metrics to establish realistic schedules:

:::note[⏱️ The 4 time metrics]
1. **Preparation time** (mise en place): Time spent gathering and preparing raw ingredients and cookware (fetching, weighing, peeling, chopping).
2. **Active time**: Cumulative hands-on duration spent executing culinary steps.
3. **Passive time**: Autonomous baking, resting, fermentation, or idle waiting time.
4. **Total time**: Preparation time + active time + passive time. Represents the overall recipe span from initial mise en place to plating.
:::

### Cheat sheet: what adds time?

Here is how the compiler converts syntax elements into working minutes:

| Syntax / Scenario | Adds to preparation time | Adds to active time | Adds to passive time |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **New ingredient** (`@flour`) | **+ 1 min** (to fetch) | - | - |
| **Intermediate** (`&dough`) | **+ 1 min** (to weigh where consumed) | - | - |
| **Prep shorthand** (`@onion(peeled)`) | **+ 2 min** | - | - |
| **Cookware** (`#pan`) | **+ 1 min** (to fetch) | - | - |
| **Active timer** (`~{10min}`) | - | **+ 10 min** | - |
| **Passive timer** (`~_{1h}`) | - | - | **+ 1 hour** (background) |
| **Step without any timer** | - | **+ 2 min** (default fallback) | - |

### When the mise en place happens
*(since v1.4.0)*

Each section has its own mise en place (gathering and preparing ingredients and cookware). Gram supports three layout strategies without requiring any changes to the recipe source text:

- **By section** (`perSection`, default): mise en place is scheduled immediately prior to that section. An ingredient needed two days later is not fetched prematurely, and preparation can occur during passive waiting times of earlier steps (masked time).
- **All at the start** (`upfront`): all prep tasks are grouped at the beginning before active cooking starts. Except for intermediate preparations, which cannot be weighed before they are produced.
- **By working day** (`perSession`): for multi-day recipes, preparation tasks for each day are grouped at the start of that day's session. Days are determined by section anchors **in days** (`~{-1d}`, `~{-2d}`). Recipes without day anchors execute in a single working day session, identical to `upfront`.

Two considerations for multi-day recipes:
- **A long passive timer is not an anchor.** A `~_{48h}` passive duration shifts the timeline two days earlier, but only an explicit section anchor formally opens a separate working day (e.g. `## Cream ~{-2d}`).
- **An anchor in hours never opens a day.** An anchor such as `~{-18h}` or `~{-36h}` represents an explicit deadline within that section's day, not an independent daily session. To schedule a previous working day, use `~{-1d}` (see [Days and hours](#days-and-hours)).

Strategy selection happens at render time: the Playground features a dropdown selector, VS Code provides the `gram.miseEnPlace` setting, the CLI exposes the `--mise-en-place` flag, and the renderer accepts `miseEnPlace`. This setting influences **total duration** and **idle time**, as well as block positioning on the Gantt chart, while keeping active preparation and hands-on cooking times invariant.

An intermediate preparation (`&dough`) is weighed in the section that consumes it and never before it is produced: even in `upfront` mode, it is scheduled as a deferred block immediately before the consuming section.

### Smart dependency tracking (ALAP)
Gram natively implements an **As Late As Possible (ALAP)** scheduling algorithm. If a dough requires `~_{1h}` passive fermentation in the background and a subsequent step depends on it, the compiler plans its kneading at the latest possible moment: fermentation finishes *exactly* when the next step begins, preventing dough from sitting over-proofed on the counter.

For a deeper architectural exploration, see the [ALAP scheduling deep dive](/docs/explanation/alap-scheduling/).

## Section retro-planning

Adding a `~{...}` annotation to a `## Section` header defines an anticipation deadline. This tells the compiler when the section must conclude relative to the final step where it is consumed.

**This acts as a temporal anchor.** An annotation like `~{-2d}` instructs the compiler to complete this section **2 full days before** it is needed in subsequent steps.

To ensure positive relative timestamps starting at `0`, the compiler normalizes the timeline: this anticipated section becomes the new start point (Time 0), and all subsequent operations are shifted proportionally. Its mise en place moves accordingly, scheduled immediately before the section, two days prior to service.

```gram
## Puff pastry ~{-2d}
```

The puff pastry must be completed **2 days** before final assembly.

### Days and hours
*(since v1.4.0)*

The chosen unit defines the anchor's semantics:

- **An anchor in days** (`~{-1d}`, `~{-2d}`) opens a distinct working day (day before, two days before), anchoring the "by working day" strategy and day labels (D-1, D-2).
- **An anchor in hours or minutes** (`~{-18h}`, `~{-90min}`) specifies a precise deadline within that section's scheduled day, without opening a new working day.

Working days are designed to fit within a 24-hour span: if a long passive duration pushes a day's work out of its window (such as a `~{-1d}` dough fermenting for 50 hours), the compiler emits `SESSION_OVERFLOW` and recommends anchoring the section further back.

### Strict syntax

Section header retro-planning annotations require a **strictly negative** signed number followed by a valid unit:

- A **required** leading `-` sign.
- A non-zero numeric value.
- A canonical unit: `d` (days), `h` (hours), or `min` (minutes), or recognized localized aliases.

```gram
## Puff pastry ~{-2d}     <!-- 2 days before -->
## Ganache ~{-30min}      <!-- 30 minutes before -->
```

Free prose (`~{the day before}`), positive values (`~{2h}`), and zero values (`~{0h}`) are invalid. Existing recipes using legacy formats still compile for backward compatibility, but produce compiler warnings.

Units resolve through the multi-language time dictionary used by `~timer`: `j`, `jour`, and `jours` are recognized aliases for `d`.

See also: [Retro-planning (Scheduling)](/docs/reference/syntax/document-structure#retro-planning-scheduling) in the document structure reference.

## Error handling

The compiler validates `~timer` declarations and section retro-planning annotations, emitting typed warnings for malformed data:

- **Missing Unit** (`~timer`): `~{30}` without units triggers `MISSING_UNIT`.
- **Invalid Unit** (`~timer`): Unrecognized units (e.g. `~{30 lightyears}`) trigger `INVALID_UNIT`.
- **Missing Unit** (section retro-planning): `~{-2}`, free text, positive (`~{2h}`), or zero values (`~{0h}`) trigger `MISSING_UNIT`.
- **Invalid Unit** (section retro-planning): Unrecognized units trigger `INVALID_UNIT`.
- **Time Paradox**: Anchors conflicting with dependency order (e.g. an ingredient anchored at `-10 min` needed by a section anchored at `-1 h`) trigger `TIME_PARADOX`.
- **Track Contention**: Concurrent passive timers delayed on the same named track trigger `TRACK_CONTENTION`.
- **Session Overflow** *(Since 1.4.0)*: Passive durations pushing working day tasks beyond the 24-hour window trigger `SESSION_OVERFLOW`.
- **Duration Out Of Range**: Durations exceeding 1,000 years are capped and trigger `DURATION_OUT_OF_RANGE`.

Warnings are non-blocking by default, but can be enforced as errors via `gram check --strict`.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/temperatures -->

You can declare thermal instructions in your recipes using the `^` symbol.

Gram supports two formats to accommodate both precise baking requirements and qualitative stovetop cooking: **Exact temperatures** and **Semantic temperatures**.

## Exact temperatures

Exact temperatures specify a numeric value accompanied by a recognized unit: `C` or `F`, case-insensitive, with or without a degree symbol (`°C`/`°F`). The compiler normalizes all valid variations to the canonical `°C`/`°F` format in its output.

**Standard exact temperature**

```gram
Preheat the #oven to ^{180°C}.

Bake at ^{350°F} until golden brown.
```
  **Appliance-labeled temperature**

Just like with `~timers`, you can assign an appliance or process name to a temperature to help renderers and tools highlight equipment setup at a glance:

```gram
Preheat the #oven to ^oven{180°C}.
```

## Semantic temperatures

For stovetop cooking, searing, or subjective heat levels where exact degree values are impractical, you can write qualitative free-text strings:

```gram
Cook on ^stove{high heat} for ~{2min}.

Turn down to ^{low heat} and let simmer.
```

:::note[Parsing distinction]
When the Gram compiler inspects a `^temperature` token:
- If the text inside the braces starts with a digit, it is parsed as an **Exact temperature** and validated against recognized temperature units.
- If it starts with non-numeric text, it is treated as a **Semantic temperature** string.
:::

## Error handling

Only Celsius and Fahrenheit temperature scales are supported. The compiler emits structured warnings when encountering malformed temperature values:

- **`MISSING_UNIT`**: Triggered when a numeric temperature is given without an explicit unit (e.g. `^{200}`).
- **`INVALID_UNIT`**: Triggered when an unsupported unit is provided (e.g. `^{200K}`). The compiler preserves the raw input as written.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/intermediate-variables -->

In complex recipes, you often create sub-components (like a dough, a sauce, or a filling) that are assembled in later stages. Gram allows you to declare these sub-components as **intermediate variables**.

Once declared, an intermediate `&variable` can be referenced, measured, or used as a baseline for relative percentage calculations.

## Variable lifecycle


1. **Declaration (`->&name`)**
   You declare the intermediate variable at the end of a step or in a section header using the `->&` arrow operator.

2. **Scoping and graph registration**
   The compiler registers the variable in the global symbol scope, calculates its cumulative produced mass, and sets up dependency links for ALAP scheduling.

3. **Downstream consumption (`&name`)**
   Subsequent steps reference the variable using `&name`, optionally specifying an extracted quantity (e.g. `&puff pastry{200g}`) or computing relative ratios (`@salt{2% &dough}`).

4. **Automatic shopping list unwrapping**
   The intermediate item is kept on the step ingredient list for cooking guidance, but automatically excluded from the shopping list — only its raw constituent ingredients are purchased.


## Declaring a variable

### Step-level declaration

When placed at the very end of a step paragraph, the variable captures everything produced in that specific step:

```gram
[Add] @flour{200g} and @water{100ml}. Mix until combined. ->&dough

[Rest] Let the &dough rest for ~_{1h}.
```

### Section-level declaration

When placed at the end of a `## Section` title, the variable captures the cumulative output of the entire section:

```gram
## Puff pastry ->&puff pastry{}

[Mix] @flour{250g}, @water{120ml}, and @salt{5g}.

[Rest] In the #fridge for ~_{1h}.

[Incorporate] The @butter{200g} by folding the dough multiple times.

// The &puff pastry variable now represents the final output of the entire section.
```

## Using a variable

To use a previously declared variable, prefix its name with `&`:

```gram
Use the &puff pastry{} to line the tart tin.
```

You can also assign a quantity to it for display purposes in the rendered recipe:

```gram
Take &puff pastry{200g} and roll it out.
```

:::note[Shopping list vs recipe ingredients]
When you use an intermediate `&variable` in a later step, it **will** appear in the recipe's ingredient list for that section, guiding the cook during execution.

However, it **will not** appear in the consolidated **shopping list**. The Gram compiler automatically unpacks the intermediate into its raw constituent ingredients (such as flour and butter) and counts those toward your grocery totals.
:::

## Advanced mechanics

### Global scoping
When a variable is declared at the section level, it enters the recipe's **global symbol scope**. You can declare a variable in the very first section and safely reference it across any subsequent section.

### Relative quantities
You can calculate an ingredient's mass as a percentage of an intermediate variable's total weight (see [Relative quantities](/docs/reference/syntax/relative-quantities)):

```gram
[Mix] The ingredients to form the dough. ->&dough

[Add] @salt{2% &dough}.
```

## Compiler diagnostics

The compiler helps you maintain clean and conflict-free code by checking variable usage:

- **`SCOPE_CONFLICT`**: Triggered if the same intermediate variable name is declared multiple times across different sections.
- **`UNUSED_VARIABLE`**: Triggered if an intermediate variable is declared with `->&` but never referenced in any downstream step.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/relative-quantities -->

In cooking, and especially in baking, precision is essential. Relying on fixed quantities can lead to unbalanced outcomes when raw produce yields vary (for example, when a single lemon yields more juice than expected).

Gram solves this by allowing you to define an `@ingredient`'s quantity dynamically as a percentage of another `@ingredient` or an intermediate `&variable`. This ensures that your recipe remains balanced regardless of real-life ingredient variations.

## Syntax

You can target either a base ingredient or an intermediate variable:

**Targeting a base ingredient (@&)**

Prefix the target ingredient's name with `@&`:

```gram
Add @flour{100g} to the bowl.

Then mix in @water{70% @&flour}. // 70g of water
```

**Pattern:** `@name{ percentage% @&TargetIngredient }`
  **Targeting an intermediate variable (&)**

Reference the target intermediate variable with `&`:

```gram
Mix the ingredients to form the dough. ->&dough

Add @salt{2% &dough}. // 2% of the total mass of the &dough variable
```

**Pattern:** `@name{ percentage% &TargetVariable }`

## Resolution rules

When the compiler resolves a relative quantity, it follows three strict scoping and calculation principles:

| Rule | Behavior | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Section scoping** | Current section only | You cannot directly target a base `@ingredient` declared in a different section. To bridge sections, capture the result into a globally scoped `&variable`. |
| **Accumulation** | Sums all occurrences | If the target `@ingredient` appears multiple times within the same section, the percentage applies to their **cumulative total**. |
| **Mass-based** | Evaluated in grams | Calculations are always performed against **physical mass in grams**. For example, 50% of "2 eggs" (each standardized at 50g) produces **50g**, not 1 egg. |

## Mass calculation rules

Because relative percentages compute ratios of physical mass, the analyzer (`@gram-lang/analyzer`) standardizes target quantities before applying the percentage:

| Target unit type | Classification | Pre-calculation logic | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Explicit mass** | [Direct] | Direct computation without conversion. | `50%` of `500g` = **250g** |
| **Volume** | [Density] | Converts volume to grams using `physical.density` from the ingredient database. | `500ml` water ➔ 500g.<br/>`50%` = **250g** |
| **Count** | [Unit weight] | Multiplies count by average `physical.unit_weight` from the ingredient database. | 2 eggs (50g ea) ➔ 100g.<br/>`50%` = **50g** |
| **Unknown unit** | [Unresolved] | Cannot infer mass. Emits a `RELATIVE_QUANTITY_UNKNOWN_MASS` warning. | Preserves formula as fallback. |

## Shopping list behavior

Because relative quantities are mathematical expressions (e.g. `125% of lemon juice`), the compiler decides how to represent them on the generated shopping list:

**Fully resolved (standard)**

When the physical mass of the target is known, the formula is evaluated completely. The resulting weight is merged seamlessly with other purchases of the same ingredient:

```text
- Sugar: 156g
```
  **Unresolved fallback (hybrid)**

If mass standardization is disabled or the target item cannot be converted (e.g. missing from `ingredients.yaml`), Gram outputs a hybrid representation combining any fixed amounts with the unresolved formula:

```text
- Sugar: 20g + (125% of lemon juice)
```

This guarantees no shopping requirements are lost, even when unit data is incomplete.

## Error handling

The compiler flags logical inconsistencies in relative definitions:

- **`RELATIVE_QUANTITY_UNRESOLVED`**: Triggered when the target ingredient or variable has not been declared earlier in the section, displaying `(20% of missing ❓)`.
- **`CIRCULAR_REFERENCE`**: Triggered if an ingredient attempts to compute a percentage of itself (e.g. `@flour{10% @&flour}`), displaying `(10% of self) ⚠️`.
- **`RELATIVE_QUANTITY_UNKNOWN_MASS`**: Emitted when the target item's physical weight cannot be determined from unit conversions or the database.

:::tip[Limits of relative quantities]
Because a relative quantity's value is derived dynamically from another ingredient, it cannot serve as a reference target for portion scaling (`--scale`) or as the 100% base for Baker's Percentages (`*`). See [Deep dive: scaling](/docs/explanation/scaling) for full details.
:::

    description="Understand how the ScaleEngine resolves relative quantities and reference scaling."
    href="/docs/explanation/scaling/"

---

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/composite-ingredients -->

In real-world cooking, recipes often require specific parts of an `@ingredient`—like the **zest** and **juice** of a lemon. 

If you write `@lemon zest` and `@lemon juice` separately, your shopping list will treat them as two completely different products. But lemons are bought whole!

To solve this, Gram introduces **Composite Ingredients**. By telling Gram that the juice and the zest both come from a parent `<@lemon`, the compiler can mathematically optimize your shopping list. If you need the juice of 2 lemons and the zest of 1 lemon, Gram understands they share the same physical source and will smartly add exactly **2 whole lemons** to your shopping list.

## Syntax

You define a composite ingredient using the `<` operator (which can be read as *"comes from"*). You simply append it right after the child `@ingredient`.

**Format**: `@childName{childQty}<@parentName{parentCost}`

- **`childName{childQty}`**: The specific part you are using in this step. Write its **full name**, parent word included (e.g., `@lemon juice{100ml}`), not a bare generic word — see [Naming the child](#naming-the-child) below for why. Like any other `@ingredient`, `{childQty}` is only required for a multi-word name.
- **`<@parentName`**: The physical item you actually buy at the store (e.g., `<@lemon`).
- **`{parentCost}`**: *(Optional)* How much of the parent is consumed to yield this child part (e.g., `{2}`). If you don't write it, it defaults to `1`.

### Naming the child

*(since v1.2.0)*

While Gram accepts a bare single-word child (`@juice<@lemon{1}`), you should write its full name instead (`@lemon juice{}<@lemon{1}`). That name becomes the ingredient's identity in the shared database (`ingredients.yaml`), used for mass standardization, nutrition, and `gram db enrich`.

Because the database only indexes the child's identifier, generic names collide: `@juice<@lemon` and `@juice<@orange` in another recipe would map to the same entry despite having nothing in common. Using the full name (`lemon juice`, `orange juice`) prevents collisions and automatically links with standalone, non-composite uses of the ingredient (e.g. `@orange juice{1l}` bought in a carton).

Reserve short names for one-off parts you don't track nutritionally. The compiler warns (`COMPOSITE_PARENT_CONFLICT`) if the same short name resolves to different parents within a recipe, and `gram db sync` detects collisions across your whole recipe collection.

### Preparation notes

Both the child and the parent can carry independent `()` preparation notes:
- **Child preparation** goes before the `<`: `@lemon juice{}(strained)<@lemon{1}`.
- **Parent preparation** goes after the cost or parent name: `@lemon juice{}<@lemon{1}(cut in half)`.

Attach the note to the part it actually describes (what is done to the extracted part vs. the whole item). You can also combine both:

```gram
Add the @lemon juice{150ml}(strained)<@lemon{1}(cut in half) to the bowl.
```

### Example

Here is how you would declare that 100ml of juice requires 2 lemons, but the zest only requires 1 lemon:

```gram
Add the @lemon juice{100ml}<@lemon{2}.

Then add the @lemon zest{1}<@lemon. // Implicitly costs 1 lemon
```
**Total required in Shopping List**: 2 Lemons.

:::caution[Strict Spacing]
Spaces are **strictly forbidden** around the `<` operator.
- ❌ `@lemon zest{1} < @lemon`
- ✅ `@lemon zest{1}<@lemon`
:::

## Calculation rules

How does the compiler actually calculate the total number of lemons you need to buy? It uses three simple rules to automatically optimize your shopping list.

### 1. The overlap rule (different parts)
If you use different parts of the same parent (like zest and juice), Gram knows they can come from the exact same physical lemon. It takes the **maximum** required amount across those parts.

```gram
Add @lemon zest{1}<@lemon.  // Needs 1 lemon

Add @lemon juice{1}<@lemon. // Needs 1 lemon
```
> 🛒 **Shopping List**: 1 Lemon (The single lemon provides both parts).

### 2. The addition rule (same part)
If you use the *same* part multiple times across different steps of your recipe, Gram adds them up. You can't magically get two zests from one lemon!

```gram
Add @lemon zest{1}<@lemon.  // Needs 1 lemon

Add @lemon zest{1}<@lemon.  // Needs another lemon
```
> 🛒 **Shopping List**: 2 Lemons.

### 3. Direct usage aggregation
If you also use the whole parent ingredient directly (e.g., cutting a whole lemon into wedges for garnish), Gram simply adds it to the optimized total.

```gram
Add @lemon zest{1}<@lemon.  // Covered by the 1st lemon

Add @lemon juice{1}<@lemon. // Covered by the 1st lemon

Cut @lemon{2} into wedges.  // Needs 2 whole lemons
```
> 🛒 **Shopping List**: 3 Lemons.

## Shopping list output

The resulting shopping list structure handles composite ingredients gracefully, allowing front-end applications to display them hierarchically.

For the example above, the JSON output would look like this:

```json
{
  "type": "composite",
  "id": "lemon",
  "name": "lemon",
  "qty": 3,
  "usage": [
    { "id": "lemon-zest", "qty": 1 },
    { "id": "lemon-juice", "qty": 1 },
    { "id": "lemon", "qty": 2, "alias": "Direct Use" }
  ]
}
```

## Section ingredient lists

Unlike the shopping list, a section's own ingredient list is flat, not nested — but it still shows which parent a composite child came from, appended in parentheses right after the child's name:

```md
**Ingredients**:
- **lemon zest** (lemon)
- **lemon juice** (lemon)
```

This parenthetical works the same regardless of how you named the child — it's what keeps a bare short name (`@zest`, `@juice`) traceable to its parent if you do use one. But it's a *display* aid only; it doesn't change the child's underlying database identity, which is why the full name is still the safer default (see [Naming the child](#naming-the-child) above).

If the parent itself also has a `()` preparation (e.g. `@lemon juice{150ml}<@lemon{1}(cut in half)`), it's folded into the same parenthetical, after the parent's name:

```md
**Ingredients**:
- **lemon juice** (lemon, cut in half)
```

The parent's preparation never appears in the shopping list — like any other preparation note, it's instructional context for the recipe, not a shopping-list attribute.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/cheatsheet -->

A concise reference guide to the Gram syntax and notation.

## Basic elements

Essential markup tokens used directly inside recipe steps:

| Element | Prefix | Syntax | Example | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ingredient** | `@` | `@name[{quantity}]` | `@flour{200g}` | Declares an ingredient. Omitting `{}` indicates no specific quantity (e.g. `@salt`). |
| **Cookware** | `#` | `#name[{quantity}]` | `#pan{2}`, `#whisk` | Specifies kitchen equipment. Omitting `{}` defaults to a single item (`1`). |
| **Timer** | `~` | `~{time}` | `~{30min}` | Defines an active cooking or preparation duration. |
| **Temperature** | `^` | `^{temperature}` | `^{180°C}`, `^{350°F}` | Declares an exact heat setting (`C` or `F`, case-insensitive). |

## Modifiers

Modifiers are placed immediately after the `@` or `#` symbol to alter behavior:

| Modifier | Meaning | Example | Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `&` | **Reference** | `@&flour` | References an ingredient declared earlier without adding it again to the shopping list. |
| `=` | **Fixed quantity** | `@=salt{1 tsp}` | Marks the quantity as fixed: it will **not** scale when portions change. |
| `?` | **Optional** | `@?thyme` | Flags the item as optional for the cook. |
| `-` | **Hidden** | `@-sugar` | Suppresses the ingredient from the generated shopping list. |
| `*` | **Baker's base** | `@*flour{500g}` | Sets the reference ingredient (100%) for baker's percentage calculations. |

## Advanced syntax

Specialized patterns for flexible culinary instructions:

| Feature | Syntax pattern | Example | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Quantity range** | `min-max` | `@eggs{2-4}` | Averaged as `3` for metrics while preserving display text. |
| **Substitutions** | `item\|alt` | `@milk{100ml}\|@water{95ml}` | Declares interchangeable alternatives. |
| **Short-hand prep** | `(...)` | `@butter{10g}(room temp)` | Notes prep techniques without cluttering names. |
| **Component alias** | `:slug` | `@dry white wine:wine{10ml}` | Displays user-friendly text while mapping to a canonical ID. |
| **Relative quantity** | `% @&target` | `@water{70% @&flour}` | Computes amount relative to a reference ingredient mass. |
| **Composite child** | `<@parent` | `@lemon zest{1}<@lemon` | Bundles parts (zest, juice) into a single shopping item. |
| **Passive timer** | `~_` | `~_{1h}` | Represents resting/rising time without blocking the cook. |
| **Named timer** | `~name{...}` | `~eggs{3min}`, `~_oven{45min}` | Queues resource-constrained steps (named tracks). |
| **Semantic temperature** | `^{text}` | `^{medium heat}`, `^{simmer}` | Expresses qualitative stove settings. |
| **Fractions** | `n/d` or Unicode | `@flour{1 1/2 cups}`, `@sugar{½ cup}` | Fully supported across imperial and metric systems. |

## Intermediate variables

Intermediate variables capture sub-components (such as doughs, sauces, or garnishes) for later assembly:

| Target | Syntax | Example | Scope |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Step-level** | `->&name` at end of step | `Mix until smooth. ->&dough` | Captures the output of that single step. |
| **Section-level** | `->&name` in section title | `## Puff Pastry ->&pastry` | Captures the combined output of the entire section. |

## Section scheduling

Retro-planning anchors schedule preparations in advance:

| Syntax | Example | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `~{-time}` | `## Preferment ~{-1d}` | Tells the scheduler this section must be completed 1 day before serving. |

---

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/syntax/ai-generation-notes -->

This page is for anything that *generates* `.gram` files rather than a person typing them by hand — an import script, a scraper, or an AI model converting an existing recipe (a website, a cookbook scan, a JSON-LD blob) into Gram. The official `gram import` command feeds the AI model it calls a system prompt (`packages/cli/src/prompts/gram-spec.ts`) that's kept manually in sync with this guidance, so treat this page as the published, human-readable version of that same knowledge.

## Restructure, don't transliterate

Traditional recipe text contains many steps that only exist because prose has no other way to express them. In Gram, most of these dissolve into the syntax itself instead of staying separate steps:

- "Cut the lemon in half" → just `@lemon{1}(cut in half)` on the ingredient that uses it.
- "Reserve the seasoning" → just `&seasoning` when it's referenced later.
- "Set aside and let cool" → just `~_{30min}` at the end of the step that produces it.

A well-generated `.gram` file often has **fewer steps** than its source, different section boundaries, and a different logical flow — a 10-step source recipe might reasonably compile down to 5 Gram steps. Preserving the original step count is not a goal; clarity is. For every source step, the question worth asking is: does this step do real cooking work, or does it only exist to set up information that Gram can express inline? If it's the latter, absorb it into the ingredient or timer that uses it instead of keeping it as its own step.

## A conversion checklist

When turning an existing recipe into `.gram`, working through these five points in order catches most structural mistakes before they happen:



1. **Structure** — Identify distinct phases (dough, filling, sauce, assembly…). Each phase with its own ingredient list is a candidate for a `## Section`. Anything that must be prepared in advance gets a retro-planning lead time (see [Document Structure](/docs/reference/syntax/document-structure#retro-planning-scheduling)).
2. **Frontmatter** — Extract `title`, `author`, `source`, `category`, `portions`, and dates from whatever metadata the source provides. Never invent a value that isn't in the source.
3. **Ingredients** — List every unique `@ingredient` using its full name with spaces (`"olive oil"`, not `"olive-oil"`). Note which ones appear more than once — the second and later mentions should use `@&`. Prefer SI units for precision, but keep `tbsp`/`tsp`/`cup` for small amounts when that's how the source expresses them. For parts of an ingredient (juice, zest, yolk…), plan the [composite syntax](/docs/reference/syntax/composite-ingredients) instead of a separate prep step.
4. **Steps** — Write each step as a paragraph with a `[Verb]` action prefix, inlining every `@ingredient`, `#cookware`, `~timer`, and `^temperature` as it's introduced. Use passive timers (`~_`) for hands-off waits (oven, resting, chilling, rising) and active timers (`~`) for anything that keeps the cook busy. If multiple passive timers must happen sequentially (one after another, e.g. baking in stages), give them the SAME NAME (`~_baking{10m}` then `~_baking{30m}`) to automatically sequence them without adding to the cook's active time.
5. **Review** — Before finalizing, check for the mistakes listed below: kebab-case names, units inside cookware braces, missing `@&` on repeat mentions, redundant `->&name` declarations, and standalone steps that only prepare an ingredient for a later step.


## Common mistakes

These are the errors that show up most often in programmatically generated `.gram` files.

### Kebab-case ingredient names

```gram
❌  @olive-oil{2 tbsp}         →   ✅  @olive oil{2 tbsp}
❌  @all-purpose-flour{250g}   →   ✅  @all purpose flour{250g}
```
Gram ingredient names are real words with spaces, not slugs. Kebab-case is an internal, database-level concept — never syntax.

### Multi-word names without `{}`

```gram
❌  Add @egg substitute and mix well.
✅  Add @egg substitute{} and mix well.

❌  X @egg substitute|@tofu and stir.
✅  X @egg substitute{}|@tofu{} and stir.
```
A multi-word `@ingredient`/`#cookware` name always needs `{}` (or `{count}` for cookware) as its closing delimiter — even when the exact quantity is unknown, use empty braces `{}`. There is no bare (no-`{}`) form for a multi-word name; the bare form only works for a single word (`@salt`, `#pan`). Without `{}`, only the first word becomes the name and everything after it silently becomes ordinary step text — inside an alternative (`|`) this now throws a hard parse error instead of silently corrupting the group.

### Units inside cookware braces

```gram
❌  #pan{20cm}      →   ✅  #pan(20cm)
❌  #bowl{large}    →   ✅  #bowl(large)
```
`#cookware` braces accept integer counts only. Dimensions, materials, and descriptions always go in parentheses — see [Cookware](/docs/reference/syntax/cookware).

### Free text where a number is required

```gram
❌  @salt{to taste}        →   ✅  @salt{}   or   @salt
❌  @flour{about 200g}     →   ✅  @flour{200g}
❌  ~{about 10 minutes}    →   ✅  ~{10min}
```
Quantities and timers need a real number (or empty braces for "to taste"); fuzzy text doesn't parse.

### Using `@&` on the first occurrence

```gram
❌  @&butter{200g}   (first time butter appears)
✅  @butter{200g}    (first declaration)
✅  @&butter{50g}    (second use, in a later step)
```

### Confusing `@&` (raw ingredient) with `&` (intermediate)

```gram
// chicken was declared as @chicken{4}, NOT as an intermediate
❌  Brown the &chicken for ~{3min}.     // & implies an intermediate that doesn't exist
✅  Brown the @&chicken for ~{3min}.    // @& = second reference to a raw ingredient

// dough was produced by a step ending with ->&dough
❌  Roll out the @&dough.              // @& implies a shopping-list ingredient
✅  Roll out the &dough.               // & = reference to the declared intermediate
```
See [Intermediate Variables](/docs/reference/syntax/intermediate-variables) for the full distinction. More generally, whenever a step transforms an ingredient into a new product referenced by name in later steps ("the seasoned chicken", "the dough"), declaring it with `->&name` avoids this ambiguity entirely.

### Standalone steps that only prepare an ingredient

```gram
❌  [Prep] Cut @lemon{1} in half. Thinly slice one half for garnish.
    [Cook] Squeeze juice from @lemon{1/2} into the pan.

✅  [Cook] Squeeze @lemon juice{}<@lemon{1}(cut in half, one half sliced for garnish) into the pan.
```
Any step whose entire purpose is "take X and do Y to it before the real step" should collapse into the ingredient reference of the step that actually uses it, using the `()` preparation shorthand — here it attaches to the composite's parent (`<@lemon{1}(...)`), since "cut in half" describes the lemon, not the juice.

### "The juice/zest/part of" phrasing instead of composite syntax

```gram
❌  the juice from @lemon{1/2}    →   ✅  @lemon juice{}<@lemon{1/2}
❌  the zest of @lemon{2}         →   ✅  @lemon zest{1}<@lemon{2}
```
[Composite ingredients](/docs/reference/syntax/composite-ingredients) keep the shopping list accurate (the overlap rule: zest + juice from the same lemon still aggregates to one lemon) and remove the need for a standalone prep step. Always give the child its **full name** (parent word included), not a bare generic word like `@juice` — a bare child name becomes its own entry in the shared ingredient database with no memory of which parent it came from, so "juice" from a lemon and "juice" from an orange elsewhere would wrongly collide into one database entry. See [Naming the child](/docs/reference/syntax/composite-ingredients#naming-the-child) for the full reasoning.

### Spaces around the composite operator

```gram
❌  @lemon zest{1} < @lemon{2}
❌  @lemon zest{1} <@lemon{2}
✅  @lemon zest{1}<@lemon{2}
```

### Attaching a composite's preparation to the wrong side

```gram
❌  @lemon juice(cut in half, one half sliced for garnish)<@lemon{1}    // says the JUICE was cut in half
✅  @lemon juice<@lemon{1}(cut in half, one half sliced for garnish)    // says the LEMON was cut in half
```
Both the child and the parent of a composite can carry their own independent `()` preparation:
- **Child's preparation** goes right after its own name (and quantity, if any).
- **Parent's preparation** goes right after `<@parentName{parentCost}`.

Attach it to whichever one it actually describes — "cut in half" happens to the whole lemon, not to the extracted juice. They can also combine when both genuinely need one: `@lemon juice{150ml}(strained)<@lemon{1}(cut in half)`.

### A redundant `->&name` when the section title already declares one

```gram
❌ ## Seasoning Mix ->&seasoning

   [Mix] @paprika{2 tsp} with @salt{1 tsp}. ->&mix1   // WRONG: the section already declares the output

✅ ## Seasoning Mix ->&seasoning

   [Mix] @paprika{2 tsp} with @salt{1 tsp}.            // no local declaration needed
```
A section-level `->&name` already captures the output of every step inside it — see [Intermediate Variables](/docs/reference/syntax/intermediate-variables#section-level-declaration).

### An active timer for passive cooking

```gram
❌  Bake for ~{45min}.        // implies the cook is actively busy for 45 minutes
✅  Bake for ~_{45min}.       // the oven does the work, the cook is free
✅  Knead for ~{10min}.       // the cook IS actively busy — an active timer is correct here
```

### A `//` comment in the middle of a step

`//` comments to the end of the line, so anything after it — including
ingredients — is silently dropped. The file still compiles, with no warning, and
is simply missing them.

```gram
❌  [Mix] Combine @flour{} // quantity not stated, @sugar{} and @salt{}.
✅  [Mix] Combine @flour{} /* quantity not stated */, @sugar{} and @salt{}.
✅  [Mix] Combine @flour{}, @sugar{} and @salt{}.  // quantities not stated
```

Inside a step, use a block comment. Keep `//` at the very end of a line, or on
a line of its own. `gram import` checks for this specific loss and refuses a
result where it happened.

<!-- Source: https://gram-lang.org/docs/reference/api/data-formats -->

The JSON shapes that flow between pipeline stages, and the YAML schema for the ingredient database. This page complements the per-package references — it illustrates what the data concretely looks like when processed by Gram functions.

## 1. The AST (`@gram-lang/parser`)

The parser transforms raw recipe text into an Abstract Syntax Tree:

**Source .gram**

```gram
---
title: 'Crepes'
---

## Batter

Mix @flour{200g} and @milk{200ml}.
```
  **RecipeAST (JSON)**

```json
{
  "type": "Recipe",
  "meta": { "title": "Crepes" },
  "children": [
    {
      "type": "Section",
      "title": "Batter",
      "retroPlanning": null,
      "intermediateDecl": null,
      "children": [
        {
          "type": "Step",
          "action": null,
          "children": [
            { "type": "Text", "value": "Mix " },
            {
              "type": "Ingredient",
              "name": "flour",
              "modifiers": [],
              "alias": null,
              "preparation": null,
              "composite": null,
              "quantity": {
                "type": "Quantity",
                "value": { "type": "single", "value": 200, "text": "200" },
                "unit": "g",
                "fixed": false
              }
            },
            { "type": "Text", "value": " and " },
            {
              "type": "Ingredient",
              "name": "milk",
              "modifiers": [],
              "quantity": {
                "type": "Quantity",
                "value": { "type": "single", "value": 200, "text": "200" },
                "unit": "ml",
                "fixed": false
              }
            },
            { "type": "Text", "value": "." }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

`getAST()` returns this structure. Byte offsets (`loc`) are omitted above for brevity — every node except `RecipeAST` carries a `loc` object. See the [parser API reference](/docs/reference/api/parser) for the complete list of node interfaces and the `ASTNodeType` enum.

## 2. Compiled & analyzed recipes (`@gram-lang/kitchen`, `@gram-lang/analyzer`)

`compile()` produces a `CompilationResult`; `analyze()` returns that same base shape enriched with physical mass conversions, baker's percentages, and nutritional metrics (`AnalyzedCompilationResult`).

**Compiled recipe (Kitchen)**

```json

        { "id": "milk", "name": "milk", "qty": 200, "unit": "ml", "_usageIds": ["2"] }

  ],
  "tasks": {
    "tasks": [
      { "id": "s0.prep", "kind": "prep", "section": 0, "duration": { "nominal": 2 }, "items": [ { "kind": "gather", "target": "ingredient", "count": 2, "duration": 2 } ], "after": [] },
      { "id": "s0.0", "kind": "step", "section": 0, "step": 0, "duration": { "nominal": 2 }, "after": [] }

  }
}
```

```json
    "totalTime": 4,
    "activeTime": 2,
    "preparationTime": 2,
    "idleTime": 0,
    "blocks": [
      { "kind": "prep", "task": "s0.prep", "section": 0, "start": 0, "end": 2 },
      { "kind": "step", "task": "s0.0", "section": 0, "step": 0, "start": 2, "end": 4 }
    ],
    "sessions": [ { "day": 0, "start": 0, "end": 4, "sections": [0] } ]
  }
}
```

*(since v1.4.0)* The compiled recipe exposes `generator` (which compiler generated it), `miseEnPlace` (operational prep tasks and durations per section), `tasks` (the neutral task graph), and `schedule` (the default theoretical schedule laid out from it; alternative schedules are generated via `layout(tasks, options)`).

:::note[Deprecated timing fields]
*(since v1.4.0)* Legacy per-step `timings` and `backgroundTasks`, along with `metrics.totalTime`, `metrics.idleTime`, and time breakdowns are deprecated: they remain populated until removed in version 2.0.0, but are omitted from the example above for clarity. The [Kitchen API reference](/docs/reference/api/kitchen) documents each field and its modern counterpart.
:::

Note the compiler's `StepToken` vocabulary inside `content`: narrative text is a bare `string`; ingredients, cookware, and intermediate references share the `Usage` structure (no `type` field, identified by the presence of an `id`); timers, temperatures, comments, and declarations each carry an explicit lowercase `type`. This distinction from the parser's PascalCase `ASTNodeType` is intentional: it describes compiled *output*, not parsed source syntax. See [How to build a custom UI](/docs/how-to/build-custom-ui) for a tutorial on consuming this structure in frontend frameworks.

## 3. Composed recipes (`@gram-lang/modules`)

When a recipe imports sub-modules via the `@use` directive, `finalizeComposed()` decorates the standard `CompilationResult` into a `ComposedCompilationResult`. It adds module metadata to both the root payload and individual spliced sections:

```json
{
  "title": "Lemon Tart",
  "modules": [
    {
      "binding": "dough",
      "uri": "/bases/sweet-pastry-dough.gram",
      "title": "Sweet Pastry Dough",
      "meta": { "title": "Sweet Pastry Dough" },
      "scaleFactor": 1.5,
      "mode": "inline"
    }
  ],
  "sections": [
    {
      "title": "Sweet Pastry Dough",
      "module": {
        "binding": "dough",
        "uri": "/bases/sweet-pastry-dough.gram",
        "title": "Sweet Pastry Dough",
        "mode": "inline"
      },
      "steps": [ "/* spliced steps from the imported module */" ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Assembly",
      "steps": [ "/* host steps */" ]
    }
  ]
}
```

- **`modules`**: Array of all imported module contributors (`ModuleInfo`), detailing local binding name, source URI, resolved scale factor, and execution mode (`"inline"` or `"stocked"`).
- **`section.module`**: Present on any section spliced in from an import (`ComposedSection`), preserving traceability for user interfaces and custom renderers.

## 4. Ingredient database (YAML)

The database passed to `validateIngredientDatabase()` or `analyze()` is a flat `Record<string, IngredientData>` keyed by ingredient slug. The `gram` CLI additionally accepts (and unwraps) an optional top-level `ingredients:` key:

**Wrapped format (gram init)**

```yaml
# With the optional wrapper (scaffolded by default via gram init)
ingredients:
  flour:
    name: "All-purpose flour"
    aliases: ["farine"]
    category: "Grains"
    physical:
      density: 0.59       # g/mL — bridges volume units ("1 cup") to mass in grams
      yield: 1.0          # fraction (0, 1] — net/gross ratio after peeling or trimming
      unit_weight: 120    # grams per "unit" (e.g. "1 flour" if used bare)
    nutrition:            # all values per 100 g of raw ingredient
      calories: 364       # in kcal
      protein: 10.3       # in grams
      carbs: 76.3         # in grams
      fat: 1.0            # in grams
      sugar: 0.3          # in grams
      fiber: 2.7          # in grams
      sodium: 2           # in milligrams (mg)
```
  **Flat format (analyze)**

```yaml
# Flat form (accepted directly by validateIngredientDatabase() and analyze())
flour:
  name: "All-purpose flour"
  physical:
    density: 0.59
```

`physical` and `nutrition` blocks are both optional — an entry without either remains valid (it simply contributes no mass or nutritional data, surfacing as `missingMassIngredients` or a `MISSING_MACROS` warning). Only `name` is strictly required. The sub-fields `nutrition.calories`, `protein`, `carbs`, and `fat` are required whenever `nutrition` is declared; `sugar`, `fiber`, `sodium`, `sat_fat`, `mono_fat`, `poly_fat`, and `alcohol` are optional.

**Units matter and must be strictly observed**: `calories` is kcal, `sodium` is in **milligrams (mg)**, and every other nutrient is in grams (g) — all evaluated per 100 g of the raw ingredient. The canonical set, units, and ordering are governed by the `NUTRIENTS` table exported by `@gram-lang/analyzer`.
